newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten attacks China's onslaught on HK rights.
newsitem.headline: Patten attacks China's onslaught on HK rights.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten said on Monday that Beijing had turned a deaf ear to Hong Kong's people by moving ahead with plans to scrap laws protecting civil liberties and democracy in the British-ruled territory.

With little more than four months left before Hong Kong reverts to Beijing's control, the Standing Committee of China's parliament, the National People's Congress, approved a plan on Sunday night to amend 25 pieces of Hong Kong legislation.
The plan includes diluting the bill of rights and replacing laws on the formation of political parties and freedom of association in this territory of 6.4 million people.

Patten said the "ill-advised proposals" were going ahead despite "the strong and consistently expressed view throughout the community that Hong Kong's civil liberties should not be rolled back in this way".
He said China's parliament was "applying the rubber stamp behind closed doors" and had been "deaf to the almost unanimous voice of the people of Hong Kong".
"There can be no illusions about the consequences of this decision," he said in a statement.

"It casts doubt on the freedoms and autonomy which have been promised to Hong Kong, and the rule of law on which they are based," Patten said. "It will cause legal confusion and invite legal challenge."
China is taking back Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, under a 1984 treaty with Britain.

The territory is to become a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China and retain its capitalist system under the deal, based on a "one country, two systems" formula designed by Chinese patriarch Deng Xioaping, who died last Wednesday.
"It undermines the credibility around the world of the 'one country, two systems' model, even before the Hong Kong SAR comes into being," Patten said.

But he said it was still not too late to mend the damage. Post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa had promised the repealed laws would be replaced with legislation that would take account of Hong Kong public opinion, Patten added.
"It is already crystal clear that what the community wants to see is the preservation of Hong Kong's current civil liberties...," he said.
